Something is conditional when it depends on a condition — a requirement, a circumstance, or a rule that must be met first. It doesn't stand alone or hold automatically. It comes with a built-in "but only if..." attached to it.

The fastest way to feel this word is to connect it to the word "if." Anything conditional is tied to an "if."

"I will help you if you ask nicely." → The help is conditional.
"She gets the job if she passes the interview." → The offer is conditional.
"The medicine works if taken on an empty stomach." → The effect is conditional.

Remove the condition, and the result may not follow. That dependency is the whole point of the word.

The sharpest way to understand "conditional" is to contrast it with its opposite: unconditional, which means no conditions, no requirements, no ifs. It is absolute and guaranteed regardless of circumstances.

  • Unconditional love = I love you no matter what. Nothing you do can change it.
  • Conditional love = I love you as long as you behave, succeed, or meet my expectations. The love depends on something.

This contrast appears everywhere. Unconditional is a promise without strings attached. Conditional always has strings.

When something is described as conditional, it usually signals that it is not yet final — it can change depending on whether the condition is fulfilled.

  • A conditional job offer or conditional university admission means: "We accept you, but only if you meet certain requirements first" — like getting specific grades, passing a background check, or submitting documents.
  • A conditional loan approval means: "We will lend you money, but only after you satisfy these criteria."
  • Conditional support means: "I support you, but not unconditionally — my support has limits or requirements."
  • Conditional release from prison means: "You can go free, but only if you follow these rules (like reporting to a parole officer)." Break the condition, and you go back.

Notice the common thread: something is being granted or promised, but not freely — only in exchange for meeting a condition.

In language, a conditional sentence expresses what happens if a particular condition is met. These sentences have two parts: the condition (the "if" part) and the result.

  • "If it rains, the match will be canceled." — The cancellation depends on rain.
  • "If I were rich, I would travel the world." — The travel depends on being rich.
  • "If you had studied, you would have passed." — Passing depended on studying.

The "if" part sets up the condition; the other part tells you what follows from it. Neither part can stand alone and give you the full meaning — they depend on each other.

In logic, a conditional statement takes the form: "If P is true, then Q follows."

Example: "If all humans are mortal, and Socrates is a human, then Socrates is mortal."

The conclusion (Socrates is mortal) is not independently guaranteed — it is conditional on the premises being true. This matters in philosophy, mathematics, and any field where precise reasoning is important: many things we accept as "true" are actually conditionally true — valid only when certain assumptions hold.

Conditional probability is the probability of something happening given that something else is already known to be true.

For example: What is the chance of drawing a King from a deck of cards, if you already know the drawn card is a face card? That "given that" changes the calculation. The probability is now conditional on the information you already have. Change the condition, and the probability changes too.

Conditional statements are one of the most fundamental building blocks of code. They tell a computer: "Do this action only if this condition is true."

```
if (temperature > 30) {
display("It's hot outside!")
}
```

The message only appears when the condition — temperature above 30 — is met. This is pure conditional logic: dependent on a test being passed.

Interestingly, when "conditional" is used in emotional or personal contexts, it often carries a slightly guarded or limiting tone — suggesting something is less generous or wholehearted than it could be.

Saying someone gives "conditional friendship" or "conditional kindness" implies there are strings attached, that the warmth isn't freely given. It subtly suggests restriction. But in technical fields — grammar, math, programming, law — the word is completely neutral. It simply describes a logical relationship.

Conditional means: not absolute, not guaranteed on its own — dependent on a condition being met first. Always linked to an "if," always implying that the outcome could differ if the circumstances were different.
